title: Develop a propagation plan for any agricultural production system

lessons.title: Propagation methods and their uses
lessons.html:
Producing new plants

Propagation is the multiplication of plants, either from seed (sexual propagation) or from parts of a plant (vegetative or asexual propagation). A propagation plan ensures the right number of healthy, true-to-type plants is ready at the right time for planting, whether for vegetables, orchards, vineyards, sugarcane, forestry or ornamentals.

Sexual propagation (seed)

  • Used for most field crops, vegetables, pastures and many indigenous plants.
  • Seedlings are genetically variable unless they are hybrids or stable cultivars.
  • Use certified seed where available for purity and germination; keep seed cool and dry.
  • Some seeds need pre-treatment: soaking, scarification or cold stratification.

Vegetative propagation

MethodTypical crops
Cuttings (stem, leaf, root)Grapevine rootstocks, sweet potato, many ornamentals, herbs
Grafting and buddingCitrus, apples, avocados, macadamias, stone fruit, grapes
LayeringSome shrubs and fruits
Division, bulbs, tubers, runnersPotatoes, strawberries, garlic, bananas (suckers)
SettsSugarcane
Tissue culture (micropropagation)Bananas, potatoes, blueberries, ornamentals, forestry clones

Vegetative propagation produces plants identical to the parent (clones), keeping valuable traits. Grafting also combines a fruiting cultivar (scion) with a rootstock chosen for vigour, soil tolerance or disease resistance.

Plant health

Many diseases spread through propagation material: citrus greening and tristeza, viruses in grapes and potatoes, bacterial diseases. Use certified, disease-tested material from registered nurseries and certification schemes. Moving some plant material between regions is regulated; check plant health requirements with the Department of Agriculture before importing or moving material.

lessons.title: Nursery management and propagation environment
lessons.html:
Creating the right conditions

Nursery infrastructure

  • Propagation house or tunnel with temperature and humidity control; mist or fog systems for cuttings.
  • Hardening-off area with shade net where plants adapt to outside conditions before planting.
  • Clean water source, tested and filtered.
  • Growing media: sterile, well-drained mixes such as composted bark, coir, peat alternatives, perlite or vermiculite.
  • Containers and trays suited to the plant and planting method.

Factors for success

  • Temperature: bottom heat speeds rooting of many cuttings.
  • Humidity: high humidity prevents cuttings drying before roots form.
  • Light: enough for photosynthesis but shaded from scorching.
  • Hygiene: clean benches, disinfected tools and trays, footbaths, restricted access.
  • Rooting hormones: registered products according to the label.

Grafting and budding practice

Match the cambium layers of scion and rootstock, tie firmly, protect from drying, and graft at the right season when the bark slips (for budding) or as recommended for the crop. Use sharp, clean knives and cut away from the body. Label every batch with cultivar, rootstock and date.

Pest and disease control

Scout weekly for damping-off, root rots, aphids, whitefly, thrips and mites. Remove diseased plants immediately. Use biological and cultural controls first and registered chemicals according to the label.

Safety

Wear gloves when handling growing media (some can carry fungi and bacteria) and chemicals. Use dust masks when mixing dry media. Keep walkways dry to prevent slips.

lessons.title: Writing the propagation plan
lessons.html:
Planning numbers and timing

Step 1: define requirements

Start from the planting plan: crop, cultivar, rootstock, number of plants and planting date. For example, 10 ha of new citrus at 800 trees per ha needs 8 000 trees.

Step 2: allow for losses

Add a margin for germination failure, poor rooting, graft failure and culling. If expected success is 80%, you need to start 8 000 ÷ 0,8 = 10 000 plants. Use your own nursery records or supplier data for success rates.

Step 3: work backwards in time

List each stage and its duration, then count back from the planting date.

StageWhat to plan
Source materialOrder certified seed, budwood or rootstocks
Sowing or striking cuttingsDate, media, trays
Grafting or transplantingLabour and skill
Growing onFertigation, pest control
Hardening offSpace, shade
Dispatch and plantingTransport, field readiness

Step 4: resources and budget

Calculate media, containers, labour hours, water, energy, chemicals and space. Cost per plant in ZAR lets you compare producing your own plants with buying from a commercial nursery.

Step 5: quality standards

Define what a saleable or plantable plant looks like: height, stem thickness, root system, graft union, free of pests and diseases.

Step 6: records

Record batch numbers, source, dates, treatments and success rates. These records improve future plans and are needed for certification and traceability.

Key points

  • Choose seed or vegetative propagation according to the crop and need for true-to-type plants.
  • Use certified, disease-free material from registered sources.
  • Control temperature, humidity, light and hygiene in the nursery.
  • Plan numbers with a loss margin and work backwards from planting date.
  • Set quality standards and keep batch records.
